posts.title: Offloading a Pixel Editor's Render Pipeline to Rust/WebAssembly
posts.excerpt: How I moved dithering, flood fill, and pixel transforms out of JavaScript and into Rust, and what actually got faster.

blocks.text: Pixel V started as a pure JavaScript app. Every tool (dither, flood fill, transforms) ran on the main thread against an ImageData buffer. It was fine at 64×64. It was not fine at 1024×1024.
Where the time actually went

Profiling showed the obvious suspects: flood fill's queue churn and the per-pixel loops in the dither pass. The less obvious cost was crossing the JS/canvas boundary: putImageData on every frame of a drag.
The Rust version isn't clever; it's the same scanline-free stack fill. The win is that the whole buffer lives in wasm linear memory, so the fill never touches the JS heap until the final blit.
The dual-canvas trick
Pairing an offscreen canvas for pixel sampling with a desynchronized onscreen canvas for GPU rendering meant the wasm module could own the pixel buffer outright. JavaScript only orchestrates.
Would I do it again? For anything that loops over pixels, yes. For tool logic and UI state, JavaScript is still the right layer; the boundary tax is real and the ergonomics matter.

posts.title: Designing a Versioned File Format Around Undo
posts.excerpt: Treating the undo stack as the file format: command-pattern snapshots, versioning, and the migration story.

blocks.text: Most editors treat the file format and the undo system as separate concerns. Pixel V's core insight is that they're the same data structure: a file is just an undo history with a cursor.
Commands as the source of truth

blocks.code:
const command = {
  v: 3,                    // schema version
  tool: "fill",
  layer: layerId,
  before: snapshotRef,      // content-addressed
  after: snapshotRef,
  meta: { x, y, color },
}

blocks.text: Every command carries a schema version. On load, a migration chain walks old commands forward, which means a two-year-old file opens with its full undo history intact.
What full snapshots buy you
Deltas are smaller, but snapshots are content-addressed and deduplicated, so the real cost is lower than it looks, and restore is O(1) instead of a replay.

posts.title: Migrating Production from Heroku to GCP Without a Maintenance Window
posts.excerpt: A cross-team migration story: dual-writes, cutover rehearsals, and the sync job we made 97% faster on the way out.

blocks.text: The brief was simple: get off Heroku. The constraint was less simple: an LP-facing product with no acceptable downtime and a finance team that reconciles against it daily.
Rehearse the cutover, not the migration

We ran the full cutover three times against staging clones before touching production. Each rehearsal surfaced something the plan missed: a connection pool ceiling, a cron that assumed Heroku's ephemeral filesystem.

blocks.code:
# cutover checklist, abridged
pg_dump --snapshot=$SNAP | gcloud sql import ...
./verify-rowcounts.sh   # every table, both sides
./replay-wal.sh         # catch up writes since snapshot
# flip DNS, watch error rates for 15 min before decommission

blocks.text: The unglamorous win: while auditing the sync job for the move, we found it re-fetching unchanged records. Fixing that cut its daily runtime by 97% and main endpoint latency from 30s to 1s.

posts.title: Building a HIPAA-Compliant Audit System on Supabase
posts.excerpt: Row-level triggers, append-only tables, and covering an entire platform's surface area without a dedicated audit service.

blocks.text: HIPAA doesn't tell you how to build an audit log; it tells you what questions you must be able to answer. Who touched this record, when, and what did they see?
Triggers over middleware
Application-level audit logging has a fatal flaw: it only covers the application. Database triggers cover every path: the API, the admin console, a developer's psql session.
The append-only property matters as much as the coverage. An audit log you can edit is a liability, not a control.
